title: Martha and Mary (Luke 10:38–42)
hookLine: one sister serves and frets, the other sits at his feet, and one thing is necessary
last: YOU CAN'T STAY ON THE MOUNTAIN.

cards: Something's on the stove, the table isn't set, the bread needs cutting, and there's more to do than time to do it. Guests are here.
In Luke's story the guest is Jesus, and a woman named Martha has welcomed him into her home. She's busy with all the serving. And her sister Mary?
Sitting on the floor at Jesus's feet. Not helping. Just listening.
Martha keeps glancing in, carrying plates, getting hotter by the minute. Finally she walks right into the room and says what she's been thinking.

teach.b: Martha doesn't go to Mary. She goes to Jesus. Lord, don't you care that my sister has left me to serve alone?
Tell her to help me. It's the same question the disciples asked in the storm: don't you care? Jesus answers gently, saying her name twice, the way you speak to someone you love.
In the Douay-Rheims: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful, and art troubled about many things: But one thing is necessary. Mary hath chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her."
Careful here is old English for full of care. Luke's word means worry, anxiety. He doesn't say the serving is bad.

He's saying: you're anxious about many things, and you're missing the one. And notice where Mary sits. At a teacher's feet is a student's place; in Acts, Paul says he was brought up at the feet of Gamaliel.
Mary takes the disciple's seat, and Jesus says it won't be taken from her.

teach.h: TWO SISTERS, TWO WAYS, ONE HOUSE.
teach.b: Some Christian writers, Saint Augustine and Saint Thomas Aquinas among them, read these sisters as two ways of life: the active and the contemplative, doing and praying. But the Church never throws Martha out.
She's a saint, with her own feast day, now shared with Mary and their brother Lazarus. And in John's Gospel, it's Martha who makes a bold statement of faith. We'll hear her soon.
Monks and nuns try to hold both sisters together: prayer and work, listening and serving.

how: Catholics keep the memorial of Saints Martha, Mary and Lazarus each July, and religious communities often describe their life as holding Martha's work and Mary's prayer together.

games.q: you're Martha. dinner for a crowd, and your sister is sitting in the other room, listening. what do you do?
o: ask Jesus to tell her to help you.
sit down next to her and let dinner burn.
games.why: she asks, don't you care? and he answers gently: “Martha, Martha… one thing is necessary.”

practice: Stop in the middle of a task, as you're doing now, in a way, and let the list in your head keep talking without answering it; just notice how many things are pulling at you.
Then let them go quiet for a moment and sit where Mary sat. If you pray, just listen; if you don't, listen to the room, to your breath. One thing.

wordCard.voice: careful. Old English for full of anxious care, the word Jesus used gently to Martha, busy with many things.

orig.note: Greek: you are anxious, you worry. Jesus's word to Martha; the King James and Douay-Rheims say careful.

carryVoice: Your line: one thing is necessary. The best part won't be taken away. That's day fifty-three.
